column1: # Cross-vantage divergences that have been investigated and explained.
# compare.mjs fails on any divergence it finds. That is the right default — but
# an archive is append-only, so a single bad minute would fail every run from
# then on, and a check that is permanently red is a check nobody reads. This
# file is how a divergence stops failing the build without disappearing.
# It cannot hide anything. Every entry here is still printed by compare.mjs, with
# this explanation attached, and the run states how many findings it covered. An
# entry matches one vantage at one minute, so it can never excuse a different
# divergence, a later one, or the same fault at another vantage. Anything not
# listed here still turns the badge red.
# Adding an entry is a claim that someone looked and understood the cause. It is
# not a way to make a red run green.
# Two of the entries below are now redundant, and are kept deliberately. Since
# 2026-08-19 compare.mjs recognises a fleet relabelling caught mid-transition and
# counts it instead of failing, so the 2026-08-18 minutes would no longer be
# reported at all. They stay because they are the evidence that prompted the
# rule, and because a rule is easier to trust beside the incident it came from.

column4: explanation

Partial API response at the Amsterdam collector: 10 nodes and 77 validators against 373 at the primary, recovering completely on the next capture. The record is internally consistent (its headline stake matches the sum of its own nodes and validators), so it is a coherent but incomplete view served to one vantage, not a divergent one. flatten.awk now withholds responses like this from the series; the raw capture is archived either way.

The BAM API degraded for all three vantages from about 04:16 to 04:23 and recovered in steps. At this minute every vantage held a torn read — the primary's own header stake (50250585.36) disagreed with the sum of its nodes (65421908.80), and Singapore's disagreed with its own too — so the node sets differ because each collector caught a different instant of the same broken response, not because they were served different views. All three captures are archived; none of them enter the series.

The same 04:16-04:23 degradation, three minutes into its recovery. Amsterdam had 13 nodes and 308 validators against the primary's 12 and 306, both far below the 15 and 377 either side of the outage; the extra node is one that had come back at one vantage and not yet at the other. Internally consistent at both, which is why it took a threshold change to catch: this capture is exactly 0.80 of the network and the exclusion rule tested for less than 0.80. That rule is now 0.88 over a wider window, and this minute is excluded from the series at both vantages.

Not a disagreement between vantages: a sub-minute sampling skew. slc-mainnet-bam-2-tee dropped out of the API for under thirty-four seconds. Amsterdam sampled at 20:56:16 and Singapore at 20:56:15, both without it (14 nodes, 369 validators); the primary sampled at 20:56:49, by which time it was back (15 nodes, 377). Every vantage agrees at 20:55 and again at 20:57, and the two witnesses agree with each other exactly. compare.mjs buckets by minute because the collectors tick on independent clocks, so a node that flickers inside one minute reads as a divergence.

The Singapore side of the same sub-minute skew: sampled at 20:56:15, thirty-four seconds before the primary, while slc-mainnet-bam-2-tee was briefly absent. Same event as the Amsterdam entry above, recorded separately because an entry covers one vantage at one minute.

Sub-minute sampling skew again, this time on stake rather than the node set. Singapore sampled at 20:50:43, eight seconds after the primary and fifteen after Amsterdam, and caught a single validator holding 803,894 SOL briefly absent: 376 validators against 377 at the other two, a stake gap of 0.56% against a 0.5% tolerance. It is back at 20:51:43. All three captures are internally consistent — every header stake matches the sum of its own nodes — so none is a torn read. The underlying network was genuinely shedding validators across this minute (380 to 379 to 377 at every vantage), and Singapore's sample landed on one further transient dip within it.

A fleet relabelling caught mid-transition, and a slower one than its seven predecessors. Where earlier relabellings flipped every suffix between two consecutive captures, this took about three minutes and passed through a state where both names were present at once — the primary saw 18 nodes at this minute against Amsterdam's 17, because lon-mainnet-bam-2-tee had appeared alongside lon-mainnet-bam-1-tee at one and not yet at the other. Stake and validator counts are identical at all three vantages throughout (142435729.25, 379 validators), so nothing about the network differed; only the instant each collector sampled. Amsterdam ticks about fifteen seconds ahead of the primary here, which is why it alone diverges: Singapore samples four seconds from the primary and agrees 100% across the whole day.

The following minute of the same transition, at its widest. Amsterdam sampled at 21:53:42 and caught twenty nodes — both ams-1 and ams-2, both sin-1 and sin-2, both lon-1 and lon-2 — while the primary sampled fifteen seconds later at 21:53:57 and saw seventeen, most of the pairs already resolved to the new name. Stake is identical to the cent at both (142435729.25) and validator counts match at 379. By 21:54 all three vantages agree on sixteen nodes under the new naming. Recorded by stats.js as an identity artifact at 21:53:57 covering 13 regions, so the events it manufactured are already excluded from the published counts.

hkg-mainnet-bam-1-tee flickered in and out of the API for about eight minutes and each collector sampled a different instant of it. Amsterdam caught it absent at 14:05:52 — 15 nodes, 378 validators, 147884034.83 SOL — while the primary sampled at 14:05:50 and saw all 16. Both records are internally consistent, so neither is a torn read; the node was genuinely gone from one response and present in the other two seconds later. The missing 1524499.65 SOL is hkg's own stake, which is why the gap reads as 1.02%.

The same node, seven minutes later, and this time the primary caught it too — but as a torn read, its header stake still reporting the full 149408534.48 against a 15-node body. Amsterdam's capture at 14:12:26 is internally consistent at 147884034.83. Singapore saw the same absence at 14:12:25. All three agree again at 14:13.

The Singapore side of the same flicker: sampled at 14:06:46 and caught hkg-mainnet-bam-1-tee absent, one minute after Amsterdam did and six before the primary. This capture is torn — the header stake reports 149408534.48 while the fifteen nodes below it sum to less. Nothing followed from that at the time: the witness vantages are archived raw and have no series to be excluded from, and until 2026-08-31 nothing compared a header against its own node list anywhere. The primary served the same torn shape at 14:12, and that one did enter the series. Both are now caught on read as incoherent captures, which is the rule this entry originally described before it existed.

Singapore at 14:12:25, matching Amsterdam's capture six seconds later and the primary's torn one at the same minute. Internally consistent at 147884034.83. The node returns for every vantage at 14:13.

hkg-mainnet-bam-1-tee dropped out of /nodes for a single capture and both witnesses caught it. Amsterdam sampled at 04:22:30 and Singapore at 04:22:28; both recorded fifteen nodes, 371 validators and 148075954.76 SOL, and both are internally coherent — each header matches the sum of its own node list, so neither is a torn read. The primary sampled at 04:22:36 and saw all sixteen. The gap is exactly the missing node and nothing else: the primary node sum at 04:21 is 149633586.74, hkg holds 1557631.98, and the difference is 148075954.76 to the cent, while 382 validators less hkg's 11 leaves 371. No node appeared in its place, so this is a drop and not a relabelling. All three vantages agree at 04:21 and again at 04:23. Why this minute is a finding when similar ones are not: compare.mjs judges the witness node set against the primary's readings at the minute either side as well as the minute itself, so an absence only surfaces when the primary recorded nothing like it anywhere in that three-minute window. Every hkg absence since 08-27 is exactly one capture long, so a witness that catches one sits inside a window where the primary saw sixteen throughout. tyo-mainnet-bam-dev-tee is absent far more often — 71 primary captures on 08-26, 68 on 08-27, 48 on 08-31 — but in runs of up to 31 consecutive captures, so both collectors sit well inside the same run and agree. What this check detects is not intermittency but disagreement about it. On the node's history, counted by region because the name is not stable: hkg ran as hkg-mainnet-bam-2-tee for all of 08-26 and most of 08-27 and as hkg-mainnet-bam-1-tee from late 08-27 on, one of the fleet relabellings already on record here. By region it was absent from 4 primary captures on 08-27, 8 on 08-28, 3 on 08-29, none on 08-30 and none on 08-31 — this minute was seen only by the witnesses. Before 08-27 the region was absent only in the sixteen captures on 07-30 and 08-04 in which the API returned no nodes at all.

The Singapore side of the same single-capture drop: sampled at 04:22:28, two seconds before Amsterdam and eight before the primary, recording the same fifteen nodes, 371 validators and 148075954.76 SOL. Internally coherent, so not a torn read. Two collectors on different continents caught the same absence within two seconds of each other while the primary, sampling eight seconds later, did not. That is about as strong as evidence gets from outside the API that the node genuinely left the response rather than either collector mis-reading it. The primary carried hkg in every one of its 1474 captures on 2026-08-31, so nothing from this minute reached the published series. That day was not free of gaps — tyo-mainnet-bam-dev-tee was missing from 48 primary captures — but that node drops out in long runs which all three vantages see alike.

A rolling fleet relabelling caught mid-step, and the one step of it that moved stake. Amsterdam sampled at 23:15:38, four seconds after the primary at 23:15:34 and six after Singapore at 23:15:32. The primary and Singapore both caught dfw-mainnet-bam-1-tee and dfw-mainnet-bam-2-tee present together — eighteen nodes — while Amsterdam caught a state neither of them sampled: dfw already resolved to -1 and dub not yet flipped, seventeen nodes. All three captures are internally coherent, each header matching the sum of its own node list, so none is a torn read. What moved: at 23:14 dfw-mainnet-bam-2-tee held 898254.34 SOL across 3 validators. At 23:15 that same total sat split across the pair — dfw-1 with 830863.34 and 2 validators, dfw-2 with 67391.00 and 1. By 23:16 the remnant was gone from the network altogether rather than folded into dfw-1, taking the BAM total from 149264865.49 and 379 validators to 149197474.49 and 378. So this is not only a rename: one validator holding 67391.00 SOL disconnected inside the handover. That is why the relabelling guard declined to forgive it. The guard requires the two vantages to report identical stake and identical validator counts at the same minute, and this pair differs by exactly that departing validator. Reporting it is the documented safe direction — it costs a review entry rather than risking a real divergence waved through as another rename. Only the node-set test fired; Amsterdam's totals sit inside the primary's three-minute window, so neither the stake nor the validator tolerance was breached. On the relabelling itself: it ran from 23:13:34 to 23:35:16, about twenty-two minutes, flipping fifteen regions in strict alphabetical order from ams to tyo, one region every one or two minutes. Slow, but not new — counting a fleet relabelling as five or more regions swapping suffix, this is the third longest of the fifteen in the archive, behind 2026-06-24 at thirty-two minutes and 2026-07-08 at twenty-seven, and a fourteen-region one took nineteen minutes the previous afternoon. What has changed is the rhythm: every fleet relabelling in August finished in four minutes or less, and both September ones so far have been slow. Only the dfw step produced any disagreement between vantages at all. The relabelling guard forgave nothing on this day — the other fourteen steps were sampled consistently enough by all three collectors that no difference arose for it to forgive.

Sub-minute sampling skew during genuine validator churn. Amsterdam sampled at 13:48:11, eight seconds after both the primary and Singapore at 13:48:03, and recorded 373 validators against their 377. Its capture is internally coherent — the header stake of 149167855.24 matches the sum of its own seventeen nodes to the cent — so it is not a torn read. The four validators absent from it are Hj2jzpAp57KyM3SmnYwJbDVrQ8tTWizMon2hhzYzwxet (196607.61), HVXXmNKkmDZbZwj74iL2Y9Wu4SyrchBoxAfFYVAktLrG (171443.48), DeepM3FDWaAb7o53rvyZk5YvHLG3FvDiVXJLRY78z51p (55405.41) and 7knvB4bbqHCKuNp3ef2hJWdwqoH6WAUi55NQt6LdRfkx (39380.06), together 462836.56 SOL, and the node-sum difference between the two captures is 462836.56 to the cent — the gap is exactly those four validators and nothing else. No node was lost: all three vantages report seventeen throughout, so this is validator churn rather than a node dropping out of the response. That the state was real rather than an Amsterdam artifact is visible in the primary own next capture: at 13:49:03 the primary carries the same reduced node total of 149167855.24, one minute after Amsterdam saw it. The stake gap is 0.31 percent, inside the 0.5 percent tolerance, which is why the validator-count test fired and the stake test did not. All three vantages agree at 13:47 and again at 13:49.

Sampling skew during the SQQ suffix transition with endpoint lag, not a clean relabelling. Amsterdam at 17:53:31 lists sqq-mainnet-bam-1-tee (1 validator, 111750.25 SOL) in addition to the primary 16-node set at 17:53:19. Its other node objects match the primary exactly. All three validator lists still contain the same 377 records, so Amsterdam nodes have advanced beyond its validator endpoint; its header is 149944019.20 and node sum 149944019.22. The primary header is also lagging: 149689732.54 against node sum 149832268.97. At 17:54 all three bodies contain 379 validators and 19 nodes, including two returning SQQ validators (208058.90 SOL); all agree on the final 16 names at 18:06. The intermediate Amsterdam set never occurs in the primary three-minute window, and unequal header stake correctly prevents automatic relabelling forgiveness. Only the node-set test fires. See reviews/2026-09-09-sqq.md and test/compare-september9.mjs for pinned archive hashes and reproduced evidence. This review preserves the discrepancy and --strict still fails it; raw data and tolerances are unchanged.

Sampling skew and endpoint lag during the Amsterdam suffix transition. Singapore at 23:52:44 retains ams-mainnet-bam-1-tee with one validator and 217351.96 SOL alongside ams-2; all other nodes exactly match the primary at 23:52:43. Singapore has 383 validator records versus the primary 384, preventing automatic relabelling forgiveness despite equal headers (151338541.41 SOL). Singapore node sum is 151555893.36, while its header and validator list have already dropped the transitioning validator. All three collectors show that validator on ams-2 and matching node sets at 23:53. See reviews/2026-09-15-ams.md and test/compare-september15.mjs. Raw records and tolerances are unchanged; strict mode still fails.

A truncated /validators list while /nodes stayed complete, caught by both remote vantages and by neither the primary nor the guards, because it never reached the primary. Amsterdam sampled at 16:21:40 and received 305 validator records against the primary's 385 four seconds later at 16:21:44. The rest of the capture is not degraded at all: its nodes array matches the primary's at all seventeen nodes, every connected_validators count and every node_stake identical to the cent, and its header reads 152421249.91 SOL and 34.6529 percent, exactly the primary's. Only the validator list differs, and it disagrees with its own header — those 305 records sum to 117289938.02 SOL and 26.6656 percent. So this is not a torn read of one response but two endpoints of the same capture disagreeing with each other. The 80 absent records are not a tail, which rules out a truncated page: 64 of the 68 on ams-mainnet-bam-2-tee (30781601.90 SOL), all 12 on pit-mainnet-bam-1-tee (3338656.65), all 3 on dfw-mainnet-bam-1-tee (882034.36) and 1 of the 43 on sin-mainnet-bam-2-tee (129018.97). Two nodes vanish from the validator list while remaining present and complete in the node list of the same record. Singapore, sampling three seconds earlier at 16:21:37, received the identical 305 records in the identical order — a strict subset of the primary's list — which is the strongest part of this: two collectors on different continents do not independently drop the same 64 Amsterdam validators, so the truncation was served, not produced here. Both recovered completely on their next capture, 385 at 16:22:40 and 16:22:37. Nothing reached the published series: the series is built from the primary, whose capture at 16:21:44 carried all 385, and every vantage agreed at 16:20 and again at 16:22. Only the validator-count test fired; the stake and node-set tests could not, since both matched exactly. Precedent for the mode, all previously recorded: the primary and Singapore at 2026-08-12T04:18 (104/145 and 104/142) inside the known 04:16-04:23 degradation, and Singapore alone at 2026-08-21T16:23:59 (314/334). This is the first instance two vantages caught simultaneously with the primary clean. Worth knowing for the guards rather than for this minute: 305/385 is 0.792, just inside the 0.8 withholding ratio in flatten.awk, and the 2026-08-21 instance at 0.94 would have passed both that guard and the 0.88 publication exclusion, because both reason about magnitude and this fault does not change the header.

The Singapore half of the same truncated /validators response; see the ams entry for this minute. Singapore sampled at 16:21:37, three seconds before Amsterdam at 16:21:40 and seven before the primary at 16:21:44, and recorded the same 305 validator records in the same order, summing to the same 117289938.02 SOL, against a header of 152421249.91 SOL and 34.6529 percent that matches the primary's exactly. Its node array is likewise identical to the primary's across all seventeen nodes. The two remote vantages receiving byte-identical truncated lists three seconds apart, while the primary four seconds later received the full 385, is what makes this server-side rather than a collector fault at either site. Recovered at 16:22:37 with 385. Nothing published: the series comes from the primary, which never saw it.
